entries.note: A word reading the same both ways, from Greek [[from:palin]], back, and [[from:dromos]], a running; early English uses linked to [[see:Ben Jonson]], [[see:William Camden]] and [[see:Henry Peacham]].
Given as a common example of a [[see:palindrome]].
Given as a common example of a [[see:palindrome]].
Given as a common example of a [[see:palindrome]].
Given as a common example of a [[see:palindrome]].
A one-humped camel known for its speed, related through Greek dromos, a running, to [[same-root:palindrome]].
Elizabethan playwright whose 1640 posthumous poetry collection lists palindromes among word puzzles, one of the earliest English uses of [[see:palindrome]].
Official whose slightly earlier text describes palindromes and ascribes them to [[see:William Camden]].
Antiquarian to whom [[see:John Philipot]] ascribed palindromes, in a collection of Camden's works possibly predating [[see:Ben Jonson]]'s.
Used [[see:palindrome]] in 1638 essays, discussing a Latin palindrome he painted above a schoolhouse door in a town of rude people.

entries.term: endure rough treatment from uncultured brutes
entries.translation: endure rough treatment from uncultured brutes
entries.note: Latin palindromic phrase that [[see:Henry Peacham]] painted above a schoolhouse door in a town full of uncultured people.
Five-by-five Latin palindrome found across Europe, including Pompeii, reading the same across and down; roughly 'the farmer Arepo holds the wheels with care'; referenced in [[see:Tenet]].
What ancient Greeks called palindromes, meaning crab-like because they move back and forth like a crab.
Text readable from multiple directions; coined in the 1980s by [[see:Douglas Hofstadter]], popularised by [[see:Peter Newell]], [[see:John Langdon]] and [[see:Scott Kim]].
Computer scientist credited with coining [[see:ambigram]] in the 1980s.
Artist and writer whose 1800s English [[see:ambigram]]s with reversible illustrations got them rolling.
[[see:ambigram]] artist of the 1970s whose work featured in Dan Brown's Angels and Demons; [[see:Robert Langdon]] is named after him.
Popularised [[see:ambigram]]s alongside [[see:John Langdon]] in the 1970s.
Main character of Dan Brown's Angels and Demons, named after ambigram artist [[from:John Langdon]].
Film full of nods to the [[see:Sator Square]], whose word tenet it takes as its title; it reportedly opens in an opera house.
Longest standard English word with 180-degree rotational symmetry, font permitting, since the M turns into a W.
A Florida lake, the longest English word with horizontal-axis symmetry if proper nouns are allowed.
Word with horizontal-axis symmetry, an alternative to [[see:Okeechobee]] if proper nouns are excluded.
A word spelling a different word backwards, like [[see:bonk]] and [[see:knob]]; hetero means different.
Reads as [[see:knob]] backwards, an example of a [[see:heteropalindrome]].
Reads as [[see:bonk]] backwards, an example of a [[see:heteropalindrome]].
Another name for a [[see:heteropalindrome]], blending the prefix of [[from:anagram]] with the ending of [[from:palindrome]].
Rob's preferred name for a [[see:heteropalindrome]]; it is [[from:palindrome]]s spelled backwards.
Paired with [[see:desserts]] as the longest [[see:semordnilap]] the hosts found.
Paired with [[see:stressed]] as the longest [[see:semordnilap]] the hosts found.
Longest palindrome in the OED, an onomatopoeic word from [[from:Ulysses]], probably made palindromic on purpose.
An 11-letter palindrome, past tense of detartrate, taking tartrate out of a juice or wine to make it less tart.
Name of a language that is itself a palindrome, a proper-name example of a [[see:palindrome]].

entries.term: T. Eliot, top bard, notes putrid tang emanating, is sad; I'd assign it a name: gnat dirt upset on drab pot toilet
entries.note: An early, surprisingly long palindromic quip by [[see:Alastair Reid]]; toilet is T. Eliot backwards.

entries.term: Able was I ere I saw Elba
entries.note: Famous palindrome sometimes attributed to [[see:Napoleon]] because of his exile to Elba, though he spoke French.
Sometimes credited with [[see:Able was I ere I saw Elba]], though as a French speaker he probably never said it.

entries.term: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
entries.note: Classic palindrome easily lengthened by adding items, such as a cat, a ham, a yak; a 1980s computer made a 540-word version.
A palindromic novel of about 31,900 words whose title is also a tongue-twister.
Palindromic poem by Demetri Martin, bookended by its title and the line [[see:Evil is a deed as I live]].

entries.term: Evil is a deed as I live
entries.note: Palindromic line that bookends Demetri Martin's poem [[see:Dammit I'm mad]].
French writer of [[see:constrained writing]] who wrote [[see:Le Grand Palindrome]], [[see:La Disparition]] and [[see:Les Revenentes]].
[[see:Georges Perec]]'s 1969 palindromic poem of over 1,300 words, beginning 'trace the unequal palindrome' and ending in a near-nonsensical reversal.
Writing under deliberately set limitations, a speciality of [[see:Georges Perec]].
[[see:Georges Perec]]'s novel written without the letter E; its English translation, A Void, also avoids E.
[[see:Georges Perec]] novel using E as its only vowel; the English version is called The Exeter Text.
[[see:Weird Al Yankovic]] song made of palindromic sentences, such as 'Lisa Bonet ate no basil' and 'Do nine men interpret? Nine men, I nod'.
Writer of [[see:Bob]], called the English-language [[see:Georges Perec]]; played by Daniel Radcliffe in a film about him.
Palindromic prime of ones, zeros and 666, named by Clifford Pickover after the demon [[from:Belphegor]].
Demon said to help people make ingenious discoveries, after whom [[see:Belphegor's prime]] is named.
A person who creates palindromes; also the name of a magazine for them.
Edinburgh Festival show where [[see:palindromist]]s teach competitive palindroming.
Annual palindrome awards spelled S-Y-M-M-Y-S, from symmetrical, announced on the palindromic date 4/20/2024 this year.
Joint third in the 2024 [[see:Symmys]] short category, by Martin Clear, about living in a snide vile villa.
Joint third in the 2024 [[see:Symmys]] short category, by Squiddy the Whale: 'Now Ned, I began on age: Biden won'.
Anthony Etherin's second-placed 2024 [[see:Symmys]] short entry: 'Too long I go no gig; no loot'.
Winner of the 2024 [[see:Symmys]] short category, about Max staggering off an egg at 6 a.m.
Anthony Etherin's 2024 [[see:Symmys]] medium winner: 'Motto: be most apt. Now I won't pat some bottom'.
Steven Fraser's 2024 [[see:Symmys]] long winner, beginning 'To new eras, to boredom' and ending 'robots, are we not?'.
Wordplay dating back to ancient Greece, popular as a witty game in Latin and English; anagrams itself rearranges into [[see:ars magna]].
Practice of anagramming names to find hidden meanings, such as rearranging [[see:Messiah]]; Jess couldn't find its etymology.
Its Hebrew letters were rearranged to yield 'he shall rejoice', an example of [[see:temurah]].
Latin phrase anagrammed to est vir qui adest, 'it is the man who is here'.
Humorous [[see:anagram]] of William Shakespeare.
Latin phrase that is an [[see:anagram]] of anagrams.
Cleverly anagrammed to 'real fun', an example of an [[see:antigram]].
Anagrammed to 'I never run to flame', an example of an [[see:antigram]].
Anagrammed to 'evil's agent', an example of an [[see:antigram]].
Famously anagrammed to 'woman Hitler'.
An [[see:anagram]] that humorously opposes or changes the original meaning, as with [[see:funeral]] and real fun.
A sentence using every letter of the alphabet in as few letters as possible, often with uncommon words, like [[see:the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog]].

entries.term: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog
entries.note: The common 35-letter [[see:pangram]]; Ripley types it in the Netflix series to check a typewriter's characteristics.

entries.term: Waltz, bad nymph, for quick jigs vex
entries.note: One of the shortest English [[see:pangram]]s.

entries.term: Glib jocks quiz nymph to vex dwarf
entries.note: One of the shortest English [[see:pangram]]s.

entries.term: Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow
entries.note: A short, easy-to-remember [[see:pangram]].

entries.term: How quickly daft jumping zebras vex
entries.note: A [[see:pangram]] using vex and jumping to cover V, X, J, M and P.

entries.original: Ésope reste ici et se repose
entries.note: A French palindrome about the writer of fables, sent in by viewers of Rob's palindrome video.
A visual Spanish palindrome about a jogging tortilla.
A depressing Russian palindrome, likened to Stone Soup.

entries.term: Is it crazy how saying sentences backwards creates backwards sentences saying how crazy it is
entries.note: Word-level palindrome reading the same with word order reversed; the hosts found no name for the form beyond palindrome sentence.
Rhetorical device from a Greek word meaning shaped like the letter X, reversing structure while changing words, as in [[see:Love without end, and without measure grace]].
Rhetorical device repeating words in reverse order, common in pithy phrases like [[see:when the going gets tough, the tough get going]].

entries.term: when the going gets tough, the tough get going
entries.note: Example of [[see:antimetabole]].

entries.term: I know what I like and I like what I know
entries.note: Example of [[see:antimetabole]].

entries.term: if you fail to prepare, you prepare to fail
entries.note: Example of [[see:antimetabole]].

entries.term: Love without end, and without measure grace
entries.note: Line from Paradise Lost given as an example of [[see:chiasmus]].

entries.term: Who dotes, yet doubts; suspects, yet strongly loves
entries.note: Shakespeare line given as an example of [[see:chiasmus]].
A silly, philosophical little palindrome.

entries.term: A dog, a panic in a pagoda
entries.note: A cute, more factual palindrome.
The phobia of palindromes, itself a palindrome, so sufferers would fear the word.
